summary: Registers media types for ECMAScript and JavaScript and sets conformance requirements for implementations, aligned with current usage. It obsoletes RFC 4329. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC says which media type name a JavaScript file should have, and what a program receiving one should do with it. It settles the question of how to read the bytes, by giving an order of checks: look for a byte order mark, then use the charset parameter if there is one, and otherwise assume UTF-8. It also explains that a file may be either an ordinary script or a module, and that the file name is often the only thing that says which.

questions: what is the javascript mime type
subtitle: The media type for JavaScript and ECMAScript, and the rules for reading a script file and knowing how it is encoded.

tldr.problem: The registration of the media types for JavaScript dated from 2006 and had drifted from practice. It also predates the module system, so it did not say how a receiving program should know whether a script file is a script or a module.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC updates the registrations so that text/javascript is the one type in common use, and it defines how an implementation decides the character encoding of a script file: a byte order mark first, then the charset parameter, then UTF-8.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 4329. Every other script media type is kept for historical reasons and marked OBSOLETE.

facts.label: Media type in common use
facts.value: text/javascript, with the intended usage COMMON

facts.label: Encoding for modules
facts.value: Module goal sources must be encoded as UTF-8; all other encodings will fail

facts.label: Encoding for scripts
facts.value: Script goal sources should be encoded as UTF-8; other schemes may be supported but are discouraged

facts.label: Byte order marks
facts.value: EF BB BF is UTF-8, FF FE is UTF-16LE and FE FF is UTF-16BE

facts.label: Fallback encoding
facts.value: UTF-8, when neither a byte order mark nor a valid charset parameter decides

facts.label: New file extension
facts.value: .mjs, whose contents should be parsed using the Module goal

today: RFC 9239 was published in May 2022 as an Informational document and obsoletes RFC 4329. It has not been obsoleted or updated since. The registration of text/javascript now carries the intended usage COMMON, and every other script media type is kept for historical purposes with the intended usage OBSOLETE.

sections.title: What the Document Covers
sections.content:
The memo describes media types for the JavaScript and ECMAScript programming languages, and refers the reader to the introduction and overview of the language specification for background on the languages themselves. It updates the descriptions and registrations for these media types to reflect existing usage on the Internet, and it provides up-to-date security considerations.

It replaces the media type registrations in RFC 4329 and updates the requirements for implementations using those media types defined there, based on current existing practices, and as a consequence it obsoletes RFC 4329.

The document defines equivalent processing requirements for the various script media types. The most widely supported media type in use is text/javascript, and all others are considered historical and obsolete aliases of it.

The types defined in the document apply to scripts written in the language specification. New editions of that specification are subject to strong obligations of backward compatibility, imposed by the standardization process of Ecma International's Technical Committee 39. As a result, JavaScript code based on an earlier edition is generally compatible with an engine adhering to a later one, and the few exceptions are documented in the specification itself under the heading on additions and changes that introduce incompatibilities with prior editions. Developers commonly use feature detection to ensure that modern features are only used when available in the current environment.
sections.plainLanguage: The language itself moves slowly and stays compatible, so a file written years ago still runs. What this RFC fixes is the packaging: the name that says what kind of file it is, and what a program should do when one arrives.

sections.title: One Media Type and a Set of Old Ones
sections.content:
The document is candid about one point. Its use of the text media type tree willfully does not align with the original intent of RFC 2045, and the reason is historical. RFC 4329 registered both the text/* and the application/* types, marking the text/* types obsolete, in order to encourage people towards application/*, matching the guidance of RFC 4288, the predecessor to RFC 6838. Since then, however, the industry widely adopted text/* anyway. The definitions in the document reflect the current state of implementation across the JavaScript ecosystem, in web browsers and in other environments such as Node.js alike, in order to guarantee backward compatibility with existing applications as much as possible. Future registrations should not view this as a repeatable precedent.

The document also states its own limits. Later editions of the language specification are not directly addressed, although it is expected that implementations will behave as if applicability were extended to them. It does not address other extensions to the specification, or scripts written in other languages. It does not define how fragment identifiers in resource identifiers for documents labelled with one of its media types are resolved, though an update may define that processing. Updates of the document may introduce new optional parameters, and implementations must consider the impact of such an update.
sections.plainLanguage: There used to be a rule that text/* was the wrong family for anything but plain text, and script files were told to live under application/ instead. The industry went the other way, so the RFC admits it and follows what people actually do, while warning that this is not a precedent for future registrations.

sections.title: Script or Module
sections.content:
To formalize support for modular programs, the language specification, starting with its 6th Edition, defines two top-level goal symbols, or roots to the abstract syntax tree: Module and Script. The Script goal represents the original structure, where the code executes in the global scope, while the Module goal represents the module system built into the language from that edition onwards.

This separation means that, in the absence of additional information, there are two possible interpretations for any given ECMAScript source text. The standards body in charge of the language, Technical Committee 39, has determined that media types are outside its scope of work. It is not possible to fully determine from content or media type alone whether a source text is meant to be parsed using the Module or Script grammar goals. Therefore, as permitted by the media types in the document, scripting environments use out-of-band information to determine which goal should be used. Some scripting environments have chosen to adopt the file extension of .mjs for this purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: JavaScript now has two ways of being written: an ordinary script, which runs in the global scope, and a module, which is more contained and can import others. The same bytes can mean either, and neither the file contents nor the media type can say which, so the decision has to come from outside the file, and the .mjs extension is the usual signal.

sections.title: How the Encoding Is Decided
sections.content:
Source text can be binary source text, meaning a textual data object that represents source text encoded using a character encoding scheme. An implementation's internal representation of source text is not considered binary source text. Implementations need to determine a character encoding scheme in order to decode binary source text, and the media types allow an optional charset parameter to specify it explicitly. In order to ensure interoperability and align with widespread implementation practice, the charset parameter is optional rather than required, despite the recommendation in BCP 13 for text/* types.

Implementations that support binary source text must support it encoded using UTF-8. Module goal sources must be encoded as UTF-8, and all other encodings will fail. Script goal sources should be encoded as UTF-8; other character encoding schemes may be supported but are discouraged. Whether U+FEFF is processed as a byte order mark signature or not depends on the host environment and is not defined by the document.

Because it is possible that implementations cannot interoperably determine a single character encoding scheme simply by complying with all the requirements of the applicable specifications, a detection algorithm is defined, which implementations apply until a single scheme is determined. First, if the binary source text is not already determined to be using a Module goal and starts with a Unicode encoding form signature, the signature determines the encoding: the octet sequences EF BB BF, FF FE and FE FF mean UTF-8, UTF-16LE and UTF-16BE. Implementations must use these sequences to determine the scheme even if the determined scheme is not supported, and if this step determines the scheme the signature octets must be ignored when decoding. Second, else, if a charset parameter is specified and its value is valid and supported by the implementation, the value determines the encoding. Third, else, the encoding is assumed to be UTF-8. If the scheme was determined to be UTF-8 by any means other than the first step and the text starts with EF BB BF, that sequence is ignored when decoding.

On error handling, the RFC leaves most specifics to the processors. If the text is determined to have been encoded using a scheme the implementation cannot process, implementations can consider the resource unsupported rather than decoding it with a different scheme. If the text uses a scheme but contains octet sequences that are not valid according to it, implementations can substitute those invalid sequences with the replacement character U+FFFD, properly encoded for the scheme, or stop processing altogether.
sections.plainLanguage: A program reading a script file has to know how the bytes are encoded before it can show the text or read the code. The RFC gives a fixed order to check: a byte order mark at the start wins, then the charset parameter if it names something the program understands, and otherwise UTF-8 is assumed. A file with a .mjs name is always UTF-8, whatever else it says.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC sets out what the language specification does not cover, so that implementers know where the unknown factors lie. The language is not intended to be computationally self-sufficient; the computational environment is expected to provide facilities that enable specific functionality, and those facilities constitute unknown factors. Derived programming languages are permitted to include additional functionality that is not described in the specification, and in particular extensions defined for the JavaScript programming language are not discussed.

Uncontrolled execution of scripts can be exceedingly dangerous. Implementations that execute scripts must give consideration to their application's threat models and those of the individual features they implement, and in particular must ensure that untrusted content is not executed in an unprotected environment. Module scripts can request the fetching and processing of additional scripts, which is called importing, and implementations that support modules need to process imported sources in the same way as scripts. There may be additional privacy and security concerns depending on where the original script and its imported modules come from: a script obtained from one host could request to import a script from another host, which could expose information about the executing environment, such as its IP address, to that other host.

The language includes facilities to loop, cause computationally complex operations or consume large amounts of memory, including facilities that allow dynamically generated source text to be executed, such as the eval function. Uncontrolled execution of such features can cause denial of service, which implementations must protect against. With the addition of SharedArrayBuffer objects in version 8, it could be possible to implement a high-resolution timer, which could lead to certain types of timing and side-channel attacks. Implementations can mitigate this, for example by disabling or removing support for SharedArrayBuffer objects, or by ensuring that shared memory is only accessible between execution contexts that have some form of mutual trust.

Two further points concern the boundary with the host. A host environment can provide facilities to access external input, and scripts that pass such input to the eval function or similar features can be vulnerable to code injection attacks, so scripts are expected to protect against such attacks. A host can also provide facilities to output computed results in a user-visible manner, and implementations must take steps to avoid confusion about the origin of those messages. Implementations are required to support UTF-8, the security considerations of which apply. Source text is expected to be in Unicode Normalization Form C, and scripts and implementations must consider the security implications of unnormalized source text and data.
sections.plainLanguage: Running a script is dangerous unless the program that runs it controls the environment it runs in, so the RFC requires that untrusted code never runs unprotected. It also flags the newer risks: a module can pull in code from another host, shared memory can be used to build a fine-grained clock for timing attacks, and passing outside input into a function that evaluates code is still a way to inject code.

sections.title: The Media Type Registrations
sections.content:
The registrations are divided into two categories: the sole media type text/javascript, which is now in common usage, and the media types that are obsolete, namely application/ecmascript, application/javascript, application/x-ecmascript, application/x-javascript, text/ecmascript, text/javascript1.0, text/javascript1.1, text/javascript1.2, text/javascript1.3, text/javascript1.4, text/javascript1.5, text/jscript, text/livescript and text/x-ecmascript.

For both categories, the published specification entry is updated to reference the language specification. A new file extension of .mjs is added to the list of file extensions, with the restriction that contents should be parsed using the Module goal. The HTML specification uses text/javascript as the default media type of ECMAScript when preparing script tags, so the intended usage of text/javascript has been moved from OBSOLETE to COMMON. IANA has added the note OBSOLETED in favor of text/javascript to all registrations except text/javascript itself, and the outdated notes about text/javascript and text/ecmascript being obsoleted in favour of other types have been removed.

Four of the legacy media types have a subtype starting with the x- prefix: application/x-ecmascript, application/x-javascript, text/x-ecmascript and text/x-javascript. These are grandfathered media types registered under Appendix A of RFC 6838; they predate BCP 178, which they violate, and are included only for backward compatibility.

The registration of text/javascript lists the file extensions .js and .mjs, the Macintosh file type code TEXT, and no magic number. Its restrictions on usage say that the .mjs file extension signals that the file represents a JavaScript module, and that execution environments relying on file extensions to determine how to process inputs parse .mjs files using the Module grammar.
sections.plainLanguage: One media type survives: text/javascript, now marked as the normal one, with .js and .mjs as its file extensions. The older names, including the ones that end in a version number, are kept in the registry marked as obsolete so that old links still resolve to something sensible.

viz.caption: THE ORDER OF CHECKS FOR THE CHARACTER ENCODING

items.label: Byte order mark
items.desc: EF BB BF means UTF-8, FF FE means UTF-16LE and FE FF means UTF-16BE. The signature decides even if that scheme is not supported, and is then ignored when decoding.

items.label: charset parameter
items.desc: Used if it is specified and its value is valid and supported by the implementation.

items.label: UTF-8
items.desc: Assumed when neither of the earlier steps decides.

viz.caption: THE TWO KINDS OF SCRIPT MEDIA TYPE
THE RISKS THE RFC CALLS OUT

items.title: Uncontrolled execution
items.text: Implementations that execute scripts must ensure that untrusted content is not executed in an unprotected environment.

items.title: Imports across hosts
items.text: A script can import a script from another host, which could expose information about the executing environment to that host.

items.title: Denial of service
items.text: The language can loop, run complex operations or consume large amounts of memory, so implementations must protect against denial of service.

items.title: Code injection
items.text: Scripts that pass host-provided input to the eval function or similar features can be vulnerable to code injection attacks.

items.title: SharedArrayBuffer
items.text: Shared memory could enable a high-resolution timer and timing attacks; implementations can disable it or restrict who can share it.
